tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

14 15 Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to 16 [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of 17 a special protocol. 18 19 If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge 20 conflict, then dstask is for you! 21 22 https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc 23 24 [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) 25 26 ## Features 27 28 - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) 29 - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! 30 - Task listing won't break with long task text 31 - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** 32 - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser 33 - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows 34 - A single statically-linked binary 35 - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. 36 37 ## Non-features 38 39 - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for 40 projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial 41 to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a 42 multi-person project tracked elsewhere. 43 44 ## Requirements 45 46 - Git 47 - A 256-color capable terminal 48 49 ## Installation 50 51 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. 52 - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). 53 - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 54 1. Enable shell completions: 55 - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. 56 - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. 57 - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 58 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 59 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: 60 - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` 61 - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` 62 63 ## PowerShell completion 64 65 Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: 66 67 ```powershell 68 dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 69 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' 70 ``` 71 72 ## Usage 73 74 Run `dstask help` for usage information. 75 76 ### Basic Commands 77 78 - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task 79 - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on 80 - `dstask start` - Start working on a task 81 - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task 82 - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete 83 - `dstask edit` - Edit a task 84 - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task 85 - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note 86 - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks 87 - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks 88 - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks 89 - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) 90 - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote 91 92 ### Task Properties 93 94 - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) 95 - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` 96 - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` 97 - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` 98 - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved 99 100 ### Contexts 101 102 Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: 103 104 ```bash 105 dstask context work 106 dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work 107 dstask # shows only work tasks 108 dstask context -- # clear context 109 ``` 110 111 ### Git Sync 112 113 Sync your tasks across devices using git: 114 115 ```bash 116 # Set up sync on first device 117 cd ~/.dstask 118 git remote add origin 119 git push -u origin master 120 121 # On other devices 122 git clone ~/.dstask 123 124 # To sync 125 dstask sync 126 ``` 127 128 ### Templates 129 130 Create task templates for recurring patterns: 131 132 ```bash 133 dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 134 dstask add from-template 135 ``` 136 137 ## Best Practices 138 139 - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. 140 - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. 141 - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. 142 - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. 143 - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. 144 - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. 145 - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. 146 - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks 147 - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task 148 - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! 149 - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context 150 151 ## Database 152 153 The default database location is: 154 155 - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` 156 - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` 157 158 It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. 159 160 ## Integration of fuzzy finders 161 162 Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to 163 search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell 164 wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: 165 166 ```bash 167 function dstask () { 168 local has_double_dash subcommand 169 170 if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then 171 has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" 172 subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" 173 if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ 174 [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] 175 then 176 command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ 177 | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ 178 | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ 179 | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" 180 return 181 fi 182 fi 183 184 command dstask "$@" 185 } 186 ``` 187 188 The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` 189 command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All 190 other commands are passed directly to dstask. 191 192 ## Alternatives 193 194 Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. 195 196 - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell 197 - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue 198 - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support 199 - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) 200 - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager 201 - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy 202 203 ## FAQ 204 205 > Does dstask encrypt tasks? 206 207 Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote 208 repository encrypted, you may consider 209 [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or 210 [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been 211 tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the 212 tools themselves. 213 214 > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? 215 216 Yes. 217 218 1. Set a context: 219 2. Run a modify command without and ID 220 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context 221 222 This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before 223 modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of 224 potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. 225 226 You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. 227 228 > Is there a GUI or web interface? 229 230 Not as part of dstask itself. However, dstask can be used as a library -- @botto 231 has started developing a web GUI, specifically to allow task management on-the-go 232 via a smartphone: . It's in early stages but 233 is meaningful as having no smartphone-based control is a blocker for a lot of people. 234 235 > Has dstask been featured in a magazine? 236 237 Yes! :-) 238 239 [releases]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases

The editor is invoked on a **temporary copy**, not the repo file. Path:

```
$TMPDIR/dstask.<uint32>.<id>-<slug>.yml      (TMPDIR defaults to /tmp)
```

- `<uint32>`: looks random but identical for two invocations within the same
  second (time-seeded). Examples seen: `578721671`, `3853250984`.
- `<slug>`: derived from the summary: lowercased, runs of whitespace collapse

  - `a  b` -> `a-b`
  - `a-b_c.d,e` -> `abcde`
  - 60 x `a` -> 21 x `a`
- Temp file mode `0600`.
- Temp file is **deleted after a successful edit or a no-change edit**, but
  **left behind on failure paths** (editor failed, invalid status, etc.).

| `dstask 1 note some text` | appends text, commits, prints confirmation | **silent no-op: exit 0, zero output, task unchanged, no commit** |
| `dstask 1 note` (no text) | opens `$EDITOR` on temp `.md` file | **prints the note verbatim to stdout** (exact bytes, no added trailing newline), exit 0; empty note prints nothing (0 bytes) |

Print mode with multiple IDs concatenates the notes with **no separator at
all** (`dstask 1 2 note` with notes `x` and `y` prints exactly `xy`).

### 2.2 Appending text (TTY mode)

- `dstask 1 note hello world` -> notes field becomes `hello world`
  (no trailing newline). Second append `more text` -> `hello world\nmore text`.
  Rule: `notes == "" ? text : notes + "\n" + text`. If the existing note ends
  with `\n` (e.g. left by an editor) this produces a blank line before the
  appended text — the `\n` is unconditional.
- Args are joined with single spaces; a single quoted arg keeps its inner
  whitespace verbatim (`note "  spaced   out  "` -> appended
  `  spaced   out  `, serialized as `notes: "hello\n  spaced   out  "`).
- Output/stdout:

```
$
Edit note 1: first task$
^[[38;5;245m[master bd7f8dd] Edit note 1: first task$
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)$
^[[0m
```

  Commit message: `Edit note <id>: <summary>` (note: "Edit note", not "Edited note").
- Operator parsing applies to the text args, per whitespace-separated ARG:
  any arg matching `+tag`, `-tag`, `project:x`, `due:...` causes
  `^[[31moperators not valid in this context^[[0m$`, exit 1, nothing appended.
  Exception: `priority:P1` is NOT treated as an operator and is stored
  verbatim. Operators embedded inside a single quoted arg (e.g. `"word +tag"`)
  are stored verbatim. `--` as an arg is swallowed (context-bypass flag);
  remaining words form the text. `/` as first text arg sends the command into
  editor mode (the rest is consumed by the `/`-note parsing), and an empty
  string arg `""` likewise means "no text" -> editor mode.

### 2.3 Editing the note in `$EDITOR` (TTY mode, no text args)

- Temp file: `$TMPDIR/dstask.<uint32>.<id>-<slug>.md` (same naming scheme as
  edit, `.md` extension, mode 0600, same cleanup rules).
- Content = the exact current note bytes (no trailing newline added; empty
  note -> empty file).
- Whatever the editor leaves is stored verbatim, including a trailing newline
  (serialized as `notes: |` block). No validation of note content.
- No change -> `Edit note <id>: <summary>` + grey `No changes detected`, no commit.
- EDITOR unset/empty/failing -> `^[[31mFailed to run $EDITOR^[[0m$`, exit 1.
- `$VISUAL` ignored (same as edit, presumably — editor path is shared).

### 2.4 Multiple/invalid IDs

- `dstask 1 2 note hello both` appends to each task, one commit per task,
  printing one `Edit note N: ...` block per task.
- `dstask 1 99 note hi`: task 1 committed, then
  `^[[31mno open task with ID 99 exists^[[0m$`, exit 1.
- No ID: `^[[31mno ID(s) specified^[[0m$`, exit 1.
- Resolved tasks are not addressable (same `no open task` error).

## 3. `open`

Help text:

```
Usage: dstask <id...> open

Open all URLs found within the task summary and notes. If you commonly have
dozens of tabs open to later action, convert them into tasks to open later with
this command.
```

### 3.1 Browser invocation

- dstask runs **`xdg-open <url>`**, once per URL, URL as a single argv.
  `$BROWSER` is NOT consulted by dstask (a `BROWSER=/tmp/script` run failed
  with `Failed to open browser` on a system without `xdg-open`; shadowing
  `xdg-open` in PATH is what gets invoked).
- On success: **no output at all** (empty stdout/stderr), exit 0.
- If `xdg-open` cannot be launched (not on PATH):
  `^[[31mFailed to open browser^[[0m$`, exit 1, no URLs opened.
- If `xdg-open` exists but exits non-zero: dstask **ignores it**, exit 0,
  no message.
- No TTY requirement; works fully piped.

### 3.2 URL extraction

- Sources: task `summary` and `notes` (help says "summary/annotations").
- **No deduplication**: the same URL twice in the summary -> opened twice;
  same URL in summary and note -> opened twice.
- **Order is nondeterministic** — repeated runs of the same task produce
  different orders (launches appear concurrent). Do not rely on order.
- Matching is a permissive URL regex (behaves like mvdan/xurls). Observed:

  | input text | opened as |
  |---|---|
  | `http://foo.org/x.` | `http://foo.org/x` (trailing `.` stripped) |
  | `http://three.com/c!` | `http://three.com/c` (trailing `!` stripped) |
  | `http://four.com/d?` | `http://four.com/d` (trailing `?` stripped) |
  | `http://five.com/e;` | `http://five.com/e` (trailing `;` stripped) |
  | `(http://two.com/b)` | `http://two.com/b` (balanced outer parens stripped) |
  | `http://ten.com/(paren)` | `http://ten.com/(paren)` (balanced inner parens kept) |
  | `http://one.com/a,b` | `http://one.com/a,b` (comma kept) |
  | `HTTP://six.com` | `HTTP://six.com` (case-insensitive match, verbatim case) |
  | `https://seven.com:8080/p`, `http://127.0.0.1:3000/local` | kept |
  | `ftp://files.example.com/f.txt` | kept (ftp scheme matched) |
  | `www.example.net` | matched without scheme |
  | `example.com`, `test.org`, `my-site.io`, `sub.domain.co.uk`, `hello.world`, `foo.local`, `end.com` | **bare domains matched** (TLD whitelist — `.world` and even `.local` match) |
  | `file.txt`, `node.js`, `a.b`, `a.bc`, `x.y`, `foo.invalidtld`, `localhost` | NOT matched |
  | `[docs](https://md.example.com)` | `https://md.example.com` |
  | `<https://angle.example.com>` | `https://angle.example.com` |
  | `"https://quoted.example.com/p"` | `https://quoted.example.com/p` (quotes stripped) |
  | `a@b.com` | `a@b.com` (email-ish, opened verbatim!) |
  | `mailto:x@y.com` | `mailto:x@y.com` (matched verbatim) |
  | `http://eleven.com/x_y-z~w` | kept (`_ - ~` fine) |

### 3.3 Errors and batches

- Task with no URLs: `^[[31mno URLs found in task 2^[[0m$` (note: task ID,
  not UUID), exit 1, nothing opened for that task.
- Batch `dstask 1 3 open` (1 has URL, 3 doesn't): task 1's URLs opened, then
  the error, exit 1. Batch stops at first failure.
- Batch `dstask 3 1 open` where 3 is unresolvable (`no open task with ID 3
  exists`): nothing opened at all.
- No ID: `^[[31mno ID(s) specified^[[0m$`, exit 1. Resolved tasks not
  addressable (`no open task with ID N exists`).
- No commit / no repo modification ever (read-only command).
